attempts.raw_response: We left Teheran in the early morning, while the stars were still bright, and the frost lay white upon the ground. Our party consisted of four persons, mounted on such horses as could be procured at short notice, and leading two baggage-mules loaded with tents and provisions. The first stage of the journey lay across a barren plain, where the road was little more than a track marked by the bones of animals that had perished in previous winters. The cold was intense, and the wind, sweeping down from the surrounding hills, cut through our garments like a knife. Before nightfall we reached a wretched village, consisting of a few mud huts, where we were glad to shelter in a stable and share barley-bread with our animals.

pair.human_continuation:
The ordinary pace is, on an average, six
to eight miles an hour, unless the horses are very bad. It was nearly
a week, however, before we rode through the gates of Ispahan, and even
this was accounted a fair performance considering the difficulties we
had to contend with.

Towards sunset the wind rose--a sharp north-easter that made face and
ears feel as if they were being flogged with stinging-nettles. It was
not until dusk that we reached Rabat Kerim, a small mud village, with
a filthy windowless post-house. But a pigstye would have been welcome
after such a ride, and the vermin which a flickering oil-lamp revealed
in hundreds, on walls and flooring, did not prevent our sleeping
soundly till morning.
pair.prefix:
"Il n'y a qu'en Perse qu'on fait des chameaus
comme cela!"

Ispahan is about seventy farsakhs distant from Teheran. The journey
has, under favourable conditions, been ridden in under two days, but
this is very unusual, and has seldom been done except for a wager by
Europeans. In our case speed was, of course, out of the question, with
the road in the state it was.

source_document.title: A Ride to India across Persia and Baluchistan by Harry De Windt
